findings.where: Screen 3 (Seen from the rotor), its read sentence for the read-through and the Book
findings.what: The read ends 'With no load, they would be zero', which tells him an unloaded motor has no slip. That is the slip screen 4 and the first trap correct, and the Book shows it without the picture's caveat. Its 'all three shrink' also follows a list of four figures. Write: 'With less load, the slip, the rotor current and the torque all shrink. Unloaded, they fall almost to zero, because a real motor still slips a little.'

findings.where: Screen 3, the note under the controls (#edge)
findings.what: '0% is the edge a real motor never quite reaches' says a motor cannot run at 0% load. What it never reaches is zero slip, so he has to read it twice. Write: 'At 0% the picture puts the rotor at ns. A real motor never quite gets there. Even unloaded, it slips a little to turn its own bearings and fan.'

findings.where: Screen 3, the words above the picture
findings.what: Nothing on the screen says the view rides on the rotor. Only the small step label says 'Seen from the rotor'. So an arrow turning about once a second, beside a '1500 rpm' readout, can be read as the field's real speed. Before the instruction, add: 'This view rides on the rotor, so the bars stand still. You see only how fast the field gains on them.'

findings.where: Screen 5 (How it behaves), the Overload row
findings.what: The row labelled Overload only describes stalling past 3.8 times rated torque. It can read as if any load up to 3.8 times rated is fine. Relabel it 'Stalling', or add a sourced line on ordinary overload: above rated load it slips more, draws more than rated current and runs hot until the overload relay trips.

findings.where: Screen 3, the picture on the four-pole setting
findings.what: On the four-pole setting the picture still draws a two-pole field, one north-south arrow. So each bar's glow pulses at half the 2.1 Hz the readout shows. Say this in the caption and in the ignores, or draw two arrows for four poles.

p is called 'the number of poles', but nothing says why more poles turn the field slower. 'Electrical degrees' is never explained. n appears in (ns − n) ÷ ns without the text naming it, so only the drawing's key does. Add 'n is the rotor's speed', and one sentence: a four-pole winding repeats its pattern twice round the stator, so the field moves half as far each cycle.

At 360 px the five readouts sit between the picture and the Load slider. To drag the slider he has to scroll the picture half out of view. Put the Load slider straight under the picture, with the readouts after it.

findings.where: Screen 3, the bars and the caption in light mode
findings.what: The words and the caption say the bars 'glow', but in light mode they turn dark grey. So 'glow' does not match what he sees. Either call it shading, as 'current in the bar' in the key already does, or make the light-mode fill look lit.

findings.where: Screen 1 (Do you still have it?), the hint for the third option
findings.what: The hint ends 'and that is what this lesson is about', which talks about the lesson itself. End it on the point instead: 'The rotor follows the field. It does not set the field's speed.'

findings.where: Screen 8 (Find the fault), the third option and the right answer's reason
findings.what: 'Its power factor is poor' is not a slip a working electrician would make. A stronger distractor would be one he could make, such as 'the overload has tripped': that drops the contactor, so the motor would be silent, not humming. The reason for the right answer could also say how to confirm a lost line: a dead fuse, or no current on one line.

findings.where: Screen 7 (Faults and tests), the Overloads row
findings.what: The Overloads row gives only the shares of failures. As a reference it should also say how an overload shows and what to check, such as the running current against the nameplate current and the overload relay's setting.
Nothing says why there is a 60 Hz choice. One sourced line, that many ships' supplies run at 60 Hz, would tell him why it matters at sea. Give it only if research finds a primary source.

findings.where: Screen 9 (Keep this), 'What it is for' and 'Where it lives'
findings.what: Both lines give the same list of pumps, fans, compressors and conveyors. 'Where it lives: Pumps' also has a stray capital. Let 'for' say what the motor does: the constant-speed workhorse, a field that turns with the rotor a little behind. Keep the list for 'where', starting with a small letter.

findings.where: Screen 9 (Keep this), the rule box and the test trap
findings.what: He cannot measure 'Rotor current frequency = slip × f' on a cage motor, and at 360 px its '× f' wraps onto a line of its own. Swap it for the nameplate check: just under 3000 rpm on 50 Hz is two poles, just under 1500 is four. Then give the test trap the figure he would use on the job: a good winding's three resistances agree within about 1%.
